title: Upward Feedback or Complaint
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece draws a sharp line between venting and genuine upward feedback. The author argues that complaints ask a leader to absorb someone else's problem, while feedback pairs a concern with a proposed fix and therefore reads as an offer to help. Leaders instinctively resent the former and welcome the latter, even when the underlying message is identical. The piece frames this as a matter of discipline: team members who want real influence with their boss need to resist the urge toward pure catharsis. It closes with a simple operating rule for anyone hoping to be heard rather than tolerated.
points: Complaints ask the leader to own and solve the problem; feedback pairs the concern with a proposed solution.
Leaders tune out complainers as self-serving, even when they privately agree with the complaint.
Never raise a criticism upward without also offering a suggestion or solution to go with it.
The habit of pure catharsis undermines a team member's ability to actually influence change.
quotes: By expressing their dissatisfaction through complaint, team members are asking the leader to own their problem or issue and to resolve it.
Leaders prefer to engage with team members who have a ready-made solution for the problem they have identified or experienced.
The distinction between a complaint and feedback is often missed by many team members because of their need for catharsis.
Make it a rule never to offer a criticism upward without a solution or suggestion to go along with it.
Talented team members don’t complain. They refuse to act as victims.
They remember that upward feedback always amplifies the solution, not the problem or the dissatisfaction.
